title: Dawson's music class: writing a scale at the board and playing cymbals
summary: Earlier theory lessons in Muskogee let Thomas write a scale at the blackboard; Dawson invites him into the band and starts him on cymbals.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: So he didn't have nothing to do but teach the band. So he wanted to get involved with something else. So he went around to different classes to see who would want to get in and do a class of music, public school music. So when he came to my class, I raised my hand. Because see, I had had...

I forgot to tell this about my early years of school in Muskogee. We had a teacher. I don't know where she come from. Her name was Mrs. Clark. And she taught us... She taught us so many... I mean, we were just young kids. Man, she was teaching the theory of music. And the reason... That's the only reason I learned as much as I did about music. There was one girl especially. Her name was Lydia. I just didn't want... For some reason, I didn't want her to know no more about music than I did. And I didn't study
piano or nothing, but just the basic part of music. I don't know I was getting crazy about it, but I took it in public school.

So when Mr. Dawson came around trying to find somebody to get in public school music, I raised my hand and got in the class. So the first day, he gave a little speech. Now, he's a young teacher, too. He's just getting his feet wet teaching. So he asked, 'Anybody know how to write a scale?' I threw up my hand." He said, 'Well, go to the blackboard.' Now, to this day, I can't honestly say what scale he asked me to write. But to me, if I can remember, it was a scale he thought was hard, either E-flat or the key of E, something with three flats or four flats, or three sharps or four sharps. But it didn't make no difference...
And you had to construct it.

Yeah. But it didn't make no difference to me what scale either. Because we learned how to make scales, and the first thing we did was write them five lines, which gave you four spaces, and you'd write the G-clef, and then the next thing you'd do is write your signature. If it's three flats, you write your flats first. And then you start on the first line and write the key of E, E-flat. If it's A-flat, you start... You don't have to write no more signatures, because that thing at the beginning donates

[sic: denotes] what the note is. See, I knew that! So I don't know... I did it so fast, I often wonder...I have often wondered what did he actually think of me. So after class he told me to stay. I thought I had got in trouble. So he asked me to stay after school. So he said, "Would you like to get in the band?" See, he didn't have too many recruits for the band either. I said, "Yes." So he said, "Well, come to the band practice," whatever day it was, Tuesday or Thursday.
I got to the band practice. And I'll bet you can't guess what instrument...the first instrument he gave me to play.

No. That was the second. He gave me a pair of cymbals. And he showed how to beat them. He said, "You hit them, and let them go away so they can ring." And the reason the cymbals were so easy, you just read along with the bass, and at the end sometimes they'd have a cymbal marking and you strike the cymbal. And that was about the easiest thing.

So after about three or four lessons, he... I think he... I really think he was testing me out to see if I was really interested in getting into music. So after about three or four band practices, he took me to the band room.
